A1.notes.Q3: Cautious about privacy. Sensitive data needs strong justification. Improving fairness is vital, even if it means a small dip in overall accuracy.
A1.notes.Q4: Explainability is key for trust & appropriate support. High explainability is ideal, but a move to moderate isn't awful if it helps more students.
A1.notes.Q5: Fairness is paramount; we can’t exacerbate existing inequalities. A small decrease in overall accuracy to ensure equitable outcomes is acceptable.
A1.notes.Q6: Personalized outreach allows tailored support. Regular check-ins are good, but not *constant* monitoring. Twice a year feels reasonable.
A1.notes.Q7: With general info, erring on the side of fewer contacts is wise to avoid overwhelming students. Personalized contact *requires* more selectivity – it's resource intensive.
A1.Q8.1: Concerned about ‘gaming’ the system - students altering behaviour just to stay off the radar. Also need to ensure interventions are genuinely helpful, not patronizing.

A2.notes.Q3: Sensitive data is a concern, but first-gen/financial aid *could* indicate systemic barriers. Need strong safeguards and justification.
A2.notes.Q4: Explainability is crucial for building trust and enabling effective advising. High explainability preferable, even with minimal gains.
A2.notes.Q5: Fairness matters a lot. A small drop in overall accuracy is acceptable if it means equitable outcomes for all students.
A2.notes.Q6: Personalized contact is best, but needs to be handled sensitively. Twice yearly feels like a good balance between support and intrusion.
A2.notes.Q7: High-touch intervention (personalized) justifies more selective outreach than a generic message. Fewer false positives are important for trust.
A2.Q8.1: How will we ensure advisors have the training to respond effectively and avoid reinforcing existing inequalities when interpreting model outputs?

A3.notes.Q3: Reluctant to add data without clear benefit, but acknowledge the value of identifying at-risk students. Sensitive attributes require very strong justification.
A3.notes.Q4: Explainability is crucial for advisors to trust the model and offer appropriate support, so prefer higher explainability even with minor accuracy losses.
A3.notes.Q5: Fairness matters hugely; perpetuating inequalities is unacceptable. A small reduction in overall identification to achieve equity is worthwhile.
A3.notes.Q6: Personalized outreach and invitation to meet are best for proactive help. Twice a year strikes a balance between support and overwhelming students.
A3.notes.Q7: Generic email ok with wider net; personalised requires more careful targeting to avoid burdening those who don't need it - less is more when intervention requires advisor time.
A3.Q8.1: The model must be regularly evaluated for bias, and its performance across different student demographics should be transparently reported. Training for advisors on interpreting the results correctly will also be essential.

S1.notes.Q3: Data privacy is really important to me, especially demographic stuff. First-gen/financial aid *could* be helpful in understanding barriers but only if it actually makes things fairer.
S1.notes.Q4: Explainability is vital for trust, but a little loss of accuracy is okay to get more understanding. Really opaque models are creepy and unhelpful.
S1.notes.Q5: Fairness *has* to be prioritised, even if it means missing some cases. The system can’t reinforce existing inequalities. Identifying students from all groups is key.
S1.notes.Q6: Generic emails feel impersonal and likely to be ignored. Personalised support or invitations to talk are much more useful, but don’t want constant contact.
S1.notes.Q7: With a general email, contacting lots of people is okay. But with personalized help, it needs to be more targeted, because advisors have limited time.
S1.Q8.1: I'm worried about the stigma attached to being 'flagged' by the system and the potential for this data to be misused later on, even if safeguards are in place now.

S2.notes.Q3: Privacy is crucial, especially for sensitive data. Using nationality feels less invasive than others, but only if it genuinely improves fairness.
S2.notes.Q4: Explainability is important for trust and student understanding, but it’s okay to sacrifice some if we get significant gains in identifying students who need help.
S2.notes.Q5: Fairness is paramount. Missing vulnerable students is worse than falsely flagging some. A small reduction in overall accuracy for fairer outcomes is acceptable.
S2.notes.Q6: Personalized support is best, but needs to be handled sensitively. Twice a year strikes a balance between checking in and overwhelming students.
S2.notes.Q7: A personalized approach merits more caution – fewer false positives are essential there, even at the cost of missing some cases.
S2.Q8.1: It's important to ensure data is anonymized and handled with care. Cultural differences in seeking help should also be considered when interpreting model results.

S3.notes.Q3: Privacy is paramount, especially regarding sensitive attributes. Disability data only acceptable if it demonstrably improves fairness.
S3.notes.Q4: Explainability is important for trust & appropriate support, but some accuracy loss is acceptable. Highly complex 'black box' models are concerning.
S3.notes.Q5: Fairness across groups is vital. Small performance hit okay if it means equitable support; missing students due to bias isn’t acceptable.
S3.notes.Q6: Personalized outreach is key, but voluntary and respectful. Too frequent contact could be intrusive; twice a year feels reasonable.
S3.notes.Q7: Generic emails are okay with broad reach. Personalized needs a more cautious approach – don't want to create unnecessary stress or falsely flag.
S3.Q8.1: The system should prioritize student agency & allow them to opt-out of data collection and/or proactive outreach.

S4.notes.Q3: I'm wary of overreach, but disability info *could* be useful if handled carefully. It feels…necessary to consider it given my own experience, but only with a significant benefit.
S4.notes.Q4: The more explainability the better. I'd accept a small loss in accuracy for High explainability, and *need* at least Moderate before considering accepting anything less.
S4.notes.Q5: Unequal outcomes are unacceptable. A slightly lower overall success rate is worth it to ensure everyone gets a fair shot. Recall is more important – we can't miss students.
S4.notes.Q6: Generic emails feel impersonal, and might be ignored. Personalized outreach *and* the option for a meeting are important. Twice a year feels manageable.
S4.notes.Q7: With a generic email, sending to too many feels intrusive. With personalised contact, balancing the numbers is crucial for advisor bandwidth and building trust.
S4.Q8.1: I worry about the potential for this system to reinforce existing biases if not carefully monitored. My previous dropout experience makes me keen on intervention but also cautious of overreach.

S5.notes.Q3: Data privacy is important, but identifying struggling students is also crucial. I’m wary of overly invasive data collection, especially given my new status here.
S5.notes.Q4: Explainability is vital. It’s hard to trust a black box, and advisors need to understand *why* someone is flagged to offer appropriate help.
S5.notes.Q5: Fairness is important. It would be unacceptable if the model disproportionately flags students from certain backgrounds. A slight decrease in overall accuracy is okay for fairer outcomes.
S5.notes.Q6: I’d prefer personalized outreach, but also want the option of speaking with an advisor. Twice a year feels frequent enough without being overbearing.
S5.notes.Q7: Personalized emails are more valuable and justify a slightly more targeted approach, avoiding unnecessary contact. Generic outreach can feel impersonal and overwhelming.
S5.Q8.1: It's important to ensure students understand *how* the model works – transparency builds trust. Also consider cultural differences in seeking help; some cultures may be less likely to reach out proactively.

S6.notes.Q3: Privacy is key, but some data useful if it genuinely helps and isn’t intrusive. Nationality/first-gen are okay *if* used to correct for bias.
S6.notes.Q4: Explainability is vital for trust. A moderate loss of accuracy is acceptable if it means students understand *why* they’re flagged.
S6.notes.Q5: Fairness matters more than maximum efficiency, but a small drop in overall identification is okay if it truly levels the playing field.
S6.notes.Q6: Personalized outreach is better – generic emails get ignored. Regular check-ins, but not overwhelming.
S6.notes.Q7: For simple info, wider net okay. Personalized help requires caution; false positives are damaging.
S6.Q8.1: The system needs careful monitoring for unintended consequences and biases. It’s crucial to remember it's just a tool, not a judgement.

S7.notes.Q3: Privacy is paramount, but acknowledging my own support needs due to dyslexia makes disability data a qualified exception. It feels wrong to use things like race or background though.
S7.notes.Q4: Explainability is important, especially at the start. Less explainable models feel like a black box and are harder to trust, even if slightly more accurate.
S7.notes.Q5: Fairness is essential. Losing 5 students is acceptable if it means ensuring equal opportunity for all groups, and prioritizing reaching those who are *most* likely to be missed.
S7.notes.Q6: Prefer a less intrusive approach initially - an email is good. But the option to connect with an advisor is also crucial if needed.
S7.notes.Q7: With general support emails, reaching more students isn't a huge risk. Personalized contact should be targeted - fewer people but better quality support. Less 'noise'.
S7.Q8.1: It feels important to ensure the model doesn’t reinforce existing biases in how different faculty handle struggling students – there might be differences across disciplines.

S8.notes.Q3: Sensitive data feels like a step too far unless there’s demonstrable fairness benefit. First-gen and financial aid are okay if they actively *reduce* bias, but not just to improve prediction.
S8.notes.Q4: Explainability is really important, especially for students who might be anxious about being flagged. I'd rather have a slightly less accurate system that people understand.
S8.notes.Q5: Fairness is critical. It’s not okay to disproportionately help some groups at the expense of others. A small dip in overall accuracy is acceptable to address this.
S8.notes.Q6: A personalized approach feels less intrusive and more supportive than a generic email. A meeting provides the best opportunity for tailored support.
S8.notes.Q7: With general info, erring on fewer contacts is okay. But with *personalized* intervention, a balance feels right – it needs to be targeted and useful.
S8.Q8.1: The system should have a clear appeals process if a student believes they've been incorrectly flagged. Transparency around the model’s limitations is also vital.

S9.notes.Q3: Privacy is crucial, especially regarding sensitive characteristics. Some data *could* be helpful if it improves ID and fairness, but I’m wary of overreach.
S9.notes.Q4: Explainability is vital for trust and ensuring appropriate support. Losing some accuracy for clarity is worth it. Complete black boxes are unacceptable.
S9.notes.Q5: Fairness matters hugely, but complete equality at the cost of helping fewer students overall isn’t ideal. Prioritize reaching those who *are* being missed.
S9.notes.Q6: Personalized support is much more impactful than generic messages. Inviting a meeting offers deeper assistance. Frequent contact feels intrusive.
S9.notes.Q7: For simple info, casting a wider net is fine. But personalized advice needs more selectivity to avoid overwhelming advisors and students. A little false negative is better than constant unwanted contact.
S9.Q8.1: The model should be regularly audited for bias and ensure data isn’t perpetuating existing inequalities. Transparency in how the system works, beyond just explainability of individual decisions, is important too.
